display_title: Official Review of Paper1665 by Reviewer uePM

content.summary_of_the_paper: The overall context is the one of imitation learning where the agent has to learn a policy that is similar to the provided examples. The authors propose a framework that allows learning from trajectories that contain “extraneous” parts, i.e., parts that are not relevant to the task at hand. What is more, they work with visual observations. In order to do so, they embed the observations and actions using a self-supervised technique called TCC. They then propose a “voting”-based procedure to filter-out the irrelevant parts of the demonstrations. They afterwards perform behavioral cloning on the remaining parts of the demonstrations.
content.main_review:
**Strengths**

The setup is interesting because it is realistic. Humans are perfectly capable of filtering out irrelevant parts of the demonstrations while it may confuse an artificial agent.

**Weaknesses**
- Method
   - There are two fundamental points I don’t understand with the method.
       - Concerning TCC: Let’s imagine you have two demonstrations. One demonstration has 50% “garbage” at the beginning and then 50% task-related content. The other one has 50% task-related content first then 50% garbage. Given my experience with TCC, aligning these two trajectories will not work and the resulting embedding will be completely off. Do you agree? If no, can you explain why, and if yes, can you then develop on the hypothesis made about the demonstrations so that the readers understand the limitations of the method.
       -Concerning UVA: Consider now you have N demonstrations that are 90% task related but all start with 10% of irrelevant content (realistic setting=> most “teaching” videos on Youtube start with a “useless” introduction/advertisement for example). If most demonstrations start with some garbage, then UVA, starting from the first frame and taking the closest neighbors will actually reject all the task-relevant content and select the garbage. Did I misunderstand? If yes, can you clarify how UVA works, if no, can you think of a trick that could help with this issue? E.g. repeating the procedure starting from different frames of the demonstrations and “averaging”? 
Can the authors explain when/how the UVA procedure ends? I think this should be in the paper.

- Related Work
  - PWIL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04678) was the first paper to use TCC to align demonstrations in the context of imitation learning and I think the authors should 1) cite this paper 2) should not claim the usage of TCC as a main contribution, or otherwise explain how different it is from PWIL.


- Experiments
    - Please report the percentage of extraneous demonstrations in each setup.
    - I don’t understand why BC fails on the learning from slides task. As the extraneous parts are within a completely different subset of the state space (the “slides” look very different). It should be able to perform correctly, by learning the correct behavior on the relevant part of the image-state-space. Maybe it is just because you affect random action to the extraneous frames? Can you try putting a single action (like zero vector) to all these extraneous frames? I feel like it is much easier to detect “irrelevant frames” if they are associated with pure noisy frames. I would say it is hard when “meaningful” actions are also performed in “irrelevant” parts of the demonstrations.
    - Can you explain why BC performance drops so much when not provided why the reference trajectory. 
    - Why is there one environment missing in table 3 and two missing in table 4?
    - As PWIL first used TCC, you could use PWIL+TCC as a baseline too. This would really show if ignoring extraneous parts helps or if a “classical” imitation learning method performs correctly.
    - Why is EIL better without reference?
    - When a reference trajectory is provided, EIL actually gets the information that this trajectory is the “good” one. I think one important missing baseline is then BC on this single trajectory. Other papers like ORIL (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13885.pdf) present methods to learn from demonstrations and unlabeled experience (that could be your extraneous demonstrations). In the “one-reference trajectory” setup, having this baseline seems really important to me given how close the setups are.
    - If the core contribution is UVA, why not testing on proprioception (without embedding) before extending to vision-based observations?
    - I would encourage you to check out https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.12034 for HP selection in the context of Imitation Learning.
- Writing
    - 4.1: “extI raneous”
    - 3.2: “loss described in …” ?
    - 3.1: “When there is one reference trajectory, … “ ? A whole paragraph is missing here?
content.summary_of_the_review: This is an interesting paper that deals with an important and understudied problem, yet, in my opinion, it requires more work, notably concerning the evaluation and the writing, before being published. I would increase my score if the authors clarify the questions I asked in "Method", if they position better w.r.t related work and solve the major issues I raised in the "Experiments" part.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer uePM
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions. Questions are addressed below one-by-one; bodies are trimmed due to comment length limits.

*I think the authors should 1) cite PWIL 2) should not claim the usage of TCC as a main contribution, or otherwise explain how different it is from PWIL.*

**Thank you for your advice, we will cite PWIL in our next revision. Our method however is different from PWIL as we deal with extraneousness and use action-conditioned TCC’s learned representations to filter out extraneous subsequences.**

*Concerning TCC: …*

**We agree that if there were only two demonstrations it would be impossible for our model to distinguish between extraneous and useful subsequences. However since a dataset usually has more than just two demonstrations, if there is less than 50% extraneousness, and they appear in uniformly, then UVA would be able to vote out the extraneousness (which have different action-conditioned TCC embeddings from the useful parts) since more than half of the demonstrations contain useful frames at a timestep. We will discuss more on that in our revision.**

*Concerning UVA: …*

**UVA ends when all videos’ current frames come to the end of the video. When some videos come to the end while others don’t, those ended videos will always select their last frame as the current frame. Since the UVA only applies to the frame after the current frames(1), all videos will come to the end after some time(no longer than the frame number of the longest video). As for the scenario, we do think it would be a great challenge if all videos come with 10% garbage at the beginning. But since those garbage aren’t about the same extraneous action, their embedding are not similar to each other, we think (1) will force all videos to come to some normal frame soon and from that on, the alignment will go on properly. However, if all videos come with the same extraneous action, we think UVA will not be able to skip them, but this is really a too demanding task for outlier detection.**

*Please report the percentage of extraneous demonstrations in each setup.*

**We are sorry for not clarifying the proportion of extraneousness. The datasets/tasks given in Table 1 all have around ~30% of extraneousness in the demonstrations (numbers vary due to different time length of demonstrations), which is not a low number.**

*I don’t understand why BC fails on the learning from slides task. …*

**We agree with you that “meaningful” actions are much more difficult to detect than “noisy” ones, so in reach, push, and stir tasks the extraneous actions inserted were meaningful (e.g. moving in a different direction in reach). We will consider trying what is suggested in our future work.**

**As for learning from slides, the extraneous slides were able to distract behavior cloning in decision making and cause it to give wrong actions for trivial situations. Once it predicts an illegal move, e.g. trying to go left in a vertical route, it is stuck at its place forever because the next observation is exactly the same, and gives the same prediction.**

*Can you explain why BC performance drops so much when not provided why the reference trajectory.*

**It’s actually a typo, the results for imitation learning are the same with/without reference video because reference video only affects the quality of alignment.**

*Why is there one environment missing in table 3 and two missing in table 4?*

**We will fill in the baseline results in our next revision.**

*As PWIL first used TCC, you could use PWIL+TCC as a baseline too. This would really show if ignoring extraneous parts helps or if a “classical” imitation learning method performs correctly.*

**Thank you for your advice. We will consider trying that in our future work.**

*Why is EIL better without reference?*

**Instead of simplifying aligning a nearest neighbor to the perfect reference, UVA generates a virtual reference in the first hand. The virtual reference seems to be better than the perfect reference as a reference and gives better matching results, possibly because it contains results from all demonstrations of the dataset.**

*…I think one important missing baseline is then BC on this single trajectory. Other papers like ORIL present methods to learn from demonstrations and unlabeled experience (that could be your extraneous demonstrations). In the “one-reference trajectory” setup, having this baseline seems really important to me given how close the setups are.*

**We believe this is a baseline we will add in our next revision.**

*If the core contribution is UVA, why not testing on proprioception (without embedding) before extending to vision-based observations?*

**Thank you for your advice, we will consider trying that in our future work.**

*I would encourage you to check out https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.12034 for HP selection in the context of Imitation Learning.*

**Thank you for your advice, we will consider trying that in our future work.**

display_title: Official Review of Paper1665 by Reviewer KUFj

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper motivates learning from demonstrations that include extraneous subsequences which are locally consistent but not relevant to the task. It introduces a method to filter out such subsequences using a temporally aligned representation. Experiments are run on simple robotics tasks (reach, push, and stir with distractor sub-trajectories) and a new “learning from slides” task (a discrete maze interspersed with irrelevant frame sequences). The proposed method effectively learns from demonstrations with extraneousness in these settings.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
* The idea of extraneousness in demonstrations is interesting.
* The paper introduces experimental settings for testing this idea.
* The proposed method makes sense and seems effective at filtering out extraneousness.

Weaknesses:
* I wonder if other (perhaps simpler) approaches could work in this setting. For example, if an observation from the environment is provided ahead of time, some simple clustering of observations from the demonstrations might work for filtering out extraneousness. Also, if a goal is specified, goal-conditioned RL or planning could work well.
* The baselines (BC, RL, TCN) perform quite weakly and it seems like there might be something wrong in these implementations or they might need tuning.
* There are several missing experimental results: there is no RL baseline in Table 3, and there are missing tasks in Table 4 and Table 5.

Baselines:
* Behavior cloning: It's unclear to me whether the behavior cloning baseline takes in the embedding or image. If it is using the embedding, I’d expect better performance. I'm surprised that its performance on the stir task in Table 4 (12%) is so much worse than it was in Table 2 (77%). The standard deviation of 51% in Table 2 seems high. I'm also not sure why behavior cloning fails at learning from slides in Table 2.
* RL: This could use more information: which algorithm, how long was it trained, and training curve plots. Section 4.3.1 says RL algorithms struggle to accomplish the reach task due to high-dimensional input. I don’t believe this reasoning and there is no analysis to support this claim.

Other experiments:
* Section 4.5 (“Ablation Study”) is not useful; these hyperparameter experiments don’t provide meaningful insight.
* The end of section 3 says we can substitute RestNet-18 with the frozen encoder. It could be nice to see this comparison.
* Results ablating the use of action vs image in the encoder could be interesting.
* Random policy performance on each task would give a better sense of difficulty. So would an additional table showing success rates when trained on demonstrations without extraneousness.

Writing suggestions:
* Figure 2 could use more explanation, e.g. description of the colors representing each video.
* The experimental questions at the beginning of Section 4 aren’t interesting. As a rule of thumb, yes/no questions aren’t great for these.
* A description of the oracle would be helpful. It’s not clear to me why it doesn’t achieve 100% success (for example in Table 2).

Miscellaneous (extraneous?):
* Figure 4: It would be nice to see this on a learning from slides video.
* Section 3.1 ends mid-sentence.
* Section 3.2: there is a typo in the nearest neighbor definition of v_j.
content.summary_of_the_review: The setting is interesting, but the baseline results are quite lacking. I think the RL baseline should do better; if it cannot do better, I’d like to see some analysis of why it fails. I’d like to see additional baselines (e.g. goal-conditioned RL, planning).

content.title: Response to Reviewer KUFj
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions. Questions are addressed below one-by-one; bodies are trimmed due to comment length limits.

*I wonder if other … approaches could work …*

**Simple clustering can be problematic since it discards the temporal information of a demonstration sequence. In the future, we will add more baselines about UVA.**

*The baselines perform weakly … wrong … or need tuning.*

**It is not surprising that most baselines perform poorly since they are not designed for extraneous demonstrations. However, we will follow your suggestion to further tune the baselines in the future revision.**

*There are missing experimental results …*

**Thank you, we will put the results in our next revision.**

*Figure 2 could use more explanation, …*

**We will further explain the figures in our next revision. Those different colors indicate the nearest neighbor of each video’s current frame in other videos, and the color selection doesn’t bear any meaning. For example, in the “election” part of Figure 2, the first column indicates that the nearest neighbor to video 2 and 3’s current frame in video 1 are both the second frame(the frame after video 1’s current frame), and the second row indicates that in video 2, the nearest neighbor to video 1’s current frame is the sixth frame, while the nearest to video 3’s is the seventh. So the second frame of video 1, the sixth frame of video 2, and the second frame of video 3 are selected to generate the new reference embedding according to voting results. Lastly, the nearest neighbors of the new reference embeddings are selected as the new current frames, as shown in the “selection” part.**

*… unclear to me whether the behavior cloning baseline takes in the embedding or image. …*

**The 12% in Table 4 was a typo, it should be the same as Table 2 (77%). The standard deviation (51%) of stir’s behavior cloning was high because there were very unstable evaluation results in the environment, sometimes sticking to the circular route and sometimes instantly flying out of it.**

**As for learning from slides, the extraneous slides were able to distract behavior cloning in decision making and cause it to give wrong actions for trivial situations. Once it predicts an illegal move, e.g. trying to go left in a vertical route, it is stuck at its place forever because the next observation is exactly the same, and gives the same prediction.**

*RL: … which algorithm, how long was it trained, training curve plots. …*

**Thank you for your advice. We described the pipeline of action-conditioned TCC -> UVA -> visual imitation learning in Section 3.2, giving the loss functions and/or exact steps of the algorithms. The duration of training depends on the number of GPUs and their VRAM available. For us with 4 GPUS of 12GB VRAM each it takes a little more than 2 days to finish the entire pipeline. Training curves and further RL description will be added to the revision.**

*Section 4.5 is not useful …*

**We will clarify the experimented hyperparameters in Section 4.5 in our next revision. The camera setting did have a significant effect on the % of extraneous frames matched (default camera angle was 50% worse than best zoom angle). The stride of action-conditioned TCC controls how long a period of time to look back into while stacking context frames in training. Its value affects the relevance between the current and context frame and thus affects training quality. The tolerance in UVA controls the aggressiveness of it.**

**Meanwhile, we agree with another reviewer that more could be experimented on, including the proportion of extraneousness in the demonstrations and the number of demonstrations in a dataset.**

*… substitute RestNet-18 with the frozen encoder. …*

**Thank you for your advice, this is a possibility we will do in the revision.**

*… ablating the use of action vs image …*

**Thank you for your advice, we also plan to do so in the revision.**

*Random policy performance …*

**We will add random policy performance in the revision. The oracle column shows success rates trained on demonstrations without extraneousness.**

*The experimental questions …*

**Thank you for your suggestion. We will modify the research questions in the revision.**

*It’s not clear to me why [the oracle] doesn’t achieve 100% …*

**The oracle was trained on a dataset without any extraneousness using behavior cloning. It doesn’t not achieve 100% performance because the BC method might fail even when expert demonstrations are given.**

*Figure 4: …learning from slides video.*

**Due to limits on length of paper, further visualizations were uploaded in the form of videos to our [home page](https://sites.google.com/view/iclr2022eil/home). These include the learning from slides EIL visualization result video.**

*Section 3.1 ends mid-sentence. Section 3.2: typo in the nearest neighbor definition.*

**Thank you for pointing out our typos, we have fixed them.**

display_title: Official Review of Paper1665 by Reviewer CDcV

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, a special scenario of imitation learning (IL) from imperfect demonstrations, IL with extraneousness,  is studied. The extraneousness means that there could be "consistent but irrelevant" subsequences existing in the demonstrations. The main idea for the proposed extraneousness-aware IL (EIL) algorithm is to filter out these undesirable subsequences by self-supervised learning. Experiments over several continuous control tasks as well as a newly proposed discrete control task are conducted to verify the effectiveness of EIL.
content.main_review:
Strengths of the paper:
- The paper studies a new setting of IL from imperfect demonstrations. As discussed in the paper, the majority of the previous researches in this area focus on IL from noisy demonstrations, under which the demonstrations could be wrong, but are always relevant to the task. In my view, the IL with extraneousness setting indeed appears in real-world applications, and it is evidently necessary to propose new techniques under this setting.

Weakness of the paper:
- In my view, the main weakness of the paper lies in experimental evaluation:
>- For the first paper to study IL with extraneousness, it is necessary to convincingly show its difference from other IL settings. For example, including state-of-the-art IL from noisy demonstrations algorithms and third-person IL algorithms as baselines. If these methods failed, the readers would notice that IL with extraneousness is a unique and challenging problem that requires new approaches to solve.
>- The results lack showing how the portion of irrelevant subsequences, as well as the number of demonstrations, affect the performance of EIL. I guess that when the portion of irrelevant subsequences gets high, and the number of demonstrations gets smaller, the problem would become more challenging. It is necessary to verify the sensitivity of EIL under these factors to show its effectiveness as well as limitations.

Further questions and suggestions:
- I wonder whether it is necessary to make the detection of irrelevant subsequences a fully self-supervised problem. I think the imitation training error may also be useful information for detecting these subsequences. While for EIL, the IL part and the self-supervised part are done separately. 

- I don't know why not share the feature-backbone part for the image encoder and the policy? Even though the paper suggests this possibility, it wasn't realized in the experiments.

- The paper needs further proofreading to fix minor errors. To list a few,
>- In Equation (1) and (2) there should be paratheses after $exp$.
>- In the first line of Section 4.1, the word "extraneous" is not correctly spelled. 
>- Part of the numbering of the tables and figures in Section 4.3.2 seems to be incorrect.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, even though the paper studies an interesting and meaningful new problem, I think the experimental part needs significant improvement as described above.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1665 by Reviewer EjrN

content.summary_of_the_paper: The manuscript proposes a method for imitative modeling, where task-irrelevant subsequences in visual demonstrations do not negatively impact learning.
content.main_review:
Section 2: Terminology. The manuscript states: "... the vast majority of work are done in the state space, which is hard, if not impossible, to be transferred to high-dimensional observations." First, "hard" and "impossible" are subjective terms, which should be replaced with more precise characterizations of the challenge in transferring methods to higher-dimensional problems. Next, the manuscript conflates 'state' in the context of control (fully-defines the system; e.g., as in state-space equations, usually of low dimension) with state in the context of an MDP (need not fully define the system; can be of arbitrary dimension). I believe the manuscript means to draw a distinction between state spaces that happen to be of lower dimensions (could be 16x16-resolution RGB images, end-effector pose, joint positions) versus high-dimensional states (e.g., "high"-resolution images, joint positions of many agents, etc.).

Section 2: The manuscript states: "Recently, Chen et al., (2021) propose to learn policies from 'in-the-wild' videos. While achieving impressive results, the videos are still curated by human without much extraneous components." This sounds a little too subjective for my liking. If making a claim about a method’s ability to ignore the unimportant content from videos with more or less "extraneous" demonstration subsequences, there should be a way of *measuring* the extraneousness. I would wonder how the manuscript arrived at the conclusion that its curated dataset is better and more realistic than in Chen et al., (2021).

Section 3.1: Why define an MDP? The MDP formulation is not used in the remainder of the manuscript. How are trajectories incorporated in the MDP?

Section 3.1 ends with "When there is one reference trajectory,". Section 3.1 is incomplete/cutoff.

Section 3.2: The manuscript states "Assume more than one demonstration sequence are given, we can match their temporal embeddings to find the most task-relevant portions of the video." Beyond this, the manuscript implicitly assumes access to a *diverse* set of demonstration sequences. It is easy to find a set of maximally-noisy (i.e., 50%) sequences that will result in perfect alignment with each other and will teach the agent extraneous behavior. Accepting that what we *really* need here is indeed a diverse set of sequences, further discussion is needed for how detect/measure/ensure that diversity.

Section 3.2: The manuscript states "In the case where a perfect reference trajectory (no noise) is available, we can match frames in other sequences to that of the reference trajectory." Under the manuscript's assumptions (e.g., no annotations), how would the model know when there is a perfect reference trajectory? The approach would not be capable of this, without some form of supervision.

Section 3.2: The manuscript should be more clear about the training paradigm: modular pre-training steps, imitation, refinement, etc. It is unclear where what losses are imposed, when.

Section 3.2: The manuscript should be more careful about the use of the term ‘temporal’, as this implies that the model has, e.g., a time-recurrent inductive bias that attempts to model the environment's transition dynamics. Where this term is used in this manuscript, only an MLP is imposed, at each time-step, with no regard to other time-steps.

Section 3.2: UVA: The UVA needs to be compared with other alignment strategies, to show its true value -- e.g., dynamic time warping, cross-attention, factorized self-attention, temporal energy-based similarity, etc.

Section 4.3: More experiments and baselines are needed. As it stands, the manuscript was not even able to compare the baseline on all tasks. More time should be taken to reimplement the baselines and benchmark, as necessary.

Section 4.3: Table 4 is an unfair comparison and provides no information, since the approach has access to a perfect reference.

Section 4.4: Figure 5: No intuition is provided. What task was being performed — qualitatively, how should we judge that an arbitrary frame is *necessarily* extraneous or not?
content.summary_of_the_review: See main review above. The manuscript has several areas that are either incomplete, lacking description and support, and lacking in experimentation; this limits one's ability to assess the value of the methodology.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer EjrN
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions. Questions are addressed below one-by-one; bodies are trimmed due to comment length limits.

*Section 2: Terminology. … "hard" and "impossible" are subjective terms, which should be replaced with more precise characterizations of the challenge in transferring methods to higher-dimensional problems. ...*

**We appreciate your suggestion and have changed the text accordingly.**

*Section 2: … I would wonder how the manuscript arrived at the conclusion that its curated dataset is better and more realistic than in Chen et al., (2021).*

**Indeed, Chen et al., 2021 conduct their experiments with a more realistic real-world dataset. However, the focus of our paper is dealing with “extraneousness”. Since something-something-v2, which is used in Chen et al., 2021, is very large-scale and does not have labels about whether it is extraneous or not, we believe our paper is more realistic in this specific perspective. We will adjust the tone and wording accordingly.**

*Section 3.1: Why define an MDP? The MDP formulation is not used in the remainder of the manuscript. How are trajectories incorporated in the MDP?*

**The Imitation Learning method doesn’t necessarily need an MDP. However, since we have also conducted RL baselines, we include it for clarification.**

*Section 3.1 ends with "When there is one reference trajectory,". Section 3.1 is incomplete/cutoff.*

**This is a typo and we’ve corrected it.**

*Section 3.2: ... Accepting that what we really need here is indeed a diverse set of sequences, further discussion is needed for how to detect/measure/ensure that diversity.*

**We agree that the algorithm is actually incapable of filtering out extraneous behavior when the proportion of extraneousness exceeds 50%. However, we also assume that if a subsequence is extraneous, it should take less than half of the demo’s time length, or else even a human would have a hard time understanding what is the dominant part of the demo.**

**As for diversity, yes we do assume that the extraneous parts appear in uniformly random timesteps of the demo. We will add more discussion on this in our next version.**

*Section 3.2: … how would the model know when there is a perfect reference trajectory? The approach would not be capable of this, without some form of supervision.*

**The model includes UVA which is unsupervised and does not need to have knowledge of whether a perfect reference trajectory exists. Meanwhile, if we do have the knowledge, we can use the perfect trajectory, so our model works either way.**

*Section 3.2: The manuscript should be more clear about the training paradigm: ...*

**We thank the reviewer for the suggestions about paper organization. For action-conditioned TCC, we use the temporal cycle consistency loss, as given in the paragraph “Action-conditioned Temporal Cycle Consistency Representation Learning” of Section 3.2; UVA is an unsupervised one-time process and doesn’t have a loss measurement; imitation learning uses l2 loss, as mentioned in paragraph “Visual Imitation Learning” of Section 3.2. We will update the paper in our revision.**

*Section 3.2: The manuscript should be more careful about the use of the term ‘temporal’, ...*

**We will clarify when we use “temporal”. The temporal part happens in our action-conditioned TCC training: While training, context frames, i.e. previous frames are stacked together with the input frame. This allows our model to look back in time while generating a representation for the current frame, and is thus temporal. We will update in our revision.**

*Section 3.2: UVA: The UVA needs to be compared with other alignment strategies, ...*

**We will add additional comparisons in our next revision.**

*Section 4.3: More experiments and baselines are needed. ...*

**Thank you, we agree and will do so in our next revision.**

*Section 4.3: Table 4 is an unfair comparison and provides no information, since the approach has access to a perfect reference.*

**Typo, The header for the second column of Table 4 should be “ EIL (Ours) w/o reference” instead of  “ EIL (Ours) w/ reference”, so our method is compared fairly with other baselines.**

*Section 4.4: Figure 5: No intuition is provided. ...*

**The idea behind is that clean demonstrations (oracle column in Table 2) lead to better training results than those with extraneous demonstrations. The datasets/tasks given in Table 1 describe the extraneousness we intentionally add into a perfect demonstration. Therefore, we know whether an arbitrary frame is extraneous or not, while the model does not. Figure 5 is a visualization that shows our model’s ability to filter out extraneousness. For real world demonstrations, we would not have any extraneousness labels either, so only improvement in trained success rate (Table 2) would show that our model is effective. For the datasets in Table 1, since we do have labels, we can visualize to see why there is such an improvement.**

content.comment: We believe all the reviews are constructive and would like to thank our reviewers. We decide to withdraw this paper, incorporate all the suggestions and revise it.
